claim: Oriented cell intercalation is an essential developmental process that shapes tissue morphologies through the directional insertion of cells between their neighbors.
source: Oriented cell intercalation is an essential developmental process that shapes tissue morphologies through the directional insertion of cells between their neighbors.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about cell intercalation.

claim: Vertices demonstrate independent sliding behaviors along cell peripheries to produce the topological deformations responsible for intercalation.
source: Here, we identify a highly novel mechanism in which vertices demonstrate independent sliding behaviors along cell peripheries to produce the topological deformations responsible for intercalation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The motion of vertices connected by contracting interfaces is not physically coupled.
source: Through systematic analysis, we find that the motion of vertices connected by contracting interfaces is not physically coupled, but instead possess strong radial coupling.
evidence: This finding is supported by cross-correlation analysis of vertex movements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Vertices possess strong radial coupling.
source: Through systematic analysis, we find that the motion of vertices connected by contracting interfaces is not physically coupled, but instead possess strong radial coupling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative analysis in Figure 2C showing correlation between radially opposed vertices.

claim: E-cadherin and Myosin II exist in previously unstudied populations at cell vertices.
source: E-cadherin and Myosin II exist in previously unstudied populations at cell vertices and undergo oscillatory cycles of accumulation and dispersion that are coordinated with changes in cell area.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1 and 6.

claim: E-cadherin and Myosin II undergo oscillatory cycles of accumulation and dispersion that are coordinated with changes in cell area.
source: E-cadherin and Myosin II exist in previously unstudied populations at cell vertices and undergo oscillatory cycles of accumulation and dispersion that are coordinated with changes in cell area.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging and cross-correlation analysis in Figures 1, 4, and 6.

claim: Peak enrichment of vertex E-cadherin/Myosin II coincides with interface length stabilization.
source: Additionally, peak enrichment of vertex E-cadherin/Myosin II coincides with interface length stabilization.
evidence: This is shown through phase-based analysis in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Asymmetric radial force balance directs the progressive, ratcheted motion of individual vertices to drive intercalation.
source: Our results suggest a model in which asymmetric radial force balance directs the progressive, ratcheted motion of individual vertices to drive intercalation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tissue elongation is essential to the shaping of an elongated body axis.
source: Tissue elongation is essential to the shaping of an elongated body axis (Keller et al., 2000; Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994), as well as the development of many internal organs, such as the palate, cochlea, gut, and kidney (Chalmers and Slack, 2000; Tudela et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2005; Lienkamp et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Epithelial cell intercalation drives elongation of the Drosophila body axis during gastrulation in a process known as germband extension.
source: Epithelial cell intercalation drives elongation of the Drosophila body axis during gastrulation, in a process known as germband extension (GBE; Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: During germband extension, cells contract shared anterior-posterior interfaces to a single point, followed by newly juxtaposed dorsal-ventral cells constructing horizontally-oriented interfaces between them.
source: The intercalary behaviors driving GBE occur through a remodeling of cell topologies, with cells contracting shared anterior-posterior (AP, vertical or T1) interfaces to a single point, followed by newly juxtaposed dorsal-ventral (DV) cells constructing horizontally-oriented interfaces between them (Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994; Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006; Collinet et al., 2015; Yu and Fernandez-Gonzalez, 2016).
evidence: This describes the T1 process and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The T1 process results in a cumulative contraction of the embryonic epithelium along the DV axis, which helps to drive a perpendicular elongation along the AP axis.
source: This is referred to as a topological T1 process, and results in a cumulative contraction of the embryonic epithelium along the DV axis, which helps to drive a perpendicular elongation along the AP axis.
evidence: This is an established understanding of how T1 processes contribute to tissue elongation.

claim: Global polarizing cues from maternal AP patterning are translated into asymmetric protein distributions at the cellular level.
source: Previous research into the genetic factors associated with GBE has shown that global polarizing cues from maternal AP patterning are translated into asymmetric protein distributions at the cellular level (Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994; Blankenship et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: At AP interfaces, Myosin II forms both supracellular cables and smaller, transient networks.
source: At AP interfaces, Myosin II forms both supracellular cables and smaller, transient networks.
evidence: This is an observation from prior research that is being referenced.

claim: Protein populations associated with adhesion (E-cadherin, ß-catenin, Bazooka/Par-3) are found enriched at non-contracting interfaces.
source: Protein populations associated with adhesion (E-cadherin, ß-catenin, Bazooka/Par-3) are found enriched at non-contracting interfaces (Blankenship et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Actomyosin networks mediate higher line tensions along AP interfaces to direct contraction.
source: This body of work led to a model in which actomyosin networks mediate higher line tensions along AP interfaces to direct contraction (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Rauzi et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes a model from previous research supported by citations.

claim: Tricellular vertices have never been comprehensively examined in the context of intercalation.
source: However, these studies have been limited to the molecular and mechanical characteristics of interfaces between two cells. The discrete regions where these interfaces overlap, tricellular vertices, have never been comprehensively examined.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature that this study addresses.

claim: Many studies on force-generation during intercalation have addressed forces oriented along the cell cortex.
source: As a result of the focus on cell-cell interfaces, many studies on force-generation during intercalation have addressed forces oriented along the cell cortex (Bertet et al., 2004; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Rauzi et al., 2008; Rauzi et al., 2010; Kasza et al., 2014; Simões et al., 2014; Collinet et al., 2015; Yu and Fernandez-Gonzalez, 2016; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of the focus of previous research supported by multiple citations.

claim: Myosin II populations are highly active and are transiently present in multiple locations in epithelial cells, including in medial and apical cell regions.
source: However, Myosin II populations are highly active and are transiently present in multiple locations in epithelial cells, including in medial and apical cell regions (Rauzi et al., 2010; Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Medial actomyosin networks drive a number of morphogenetic processes by mediating oscillations in cell area.
source: These medial actomyosin networks drive a number of morphogenetic processes by mediating oscillations in cell area (Martin et al., 2009; Roh-Johnson et al., 2012; Simões et al., 2017; An et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During GBE, medial Myosin II flows direct apical area oscillations that contribute to AP/DV anisotropy within a cell.
source: Indeed, during GBE medial Myosin II flows direct apical area oscillations that contribute to AP/DV anisotropy within a cell (Rauzi et al., 2010; Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: E-cadherin was highly enriched at vertices at the onset of intercalation.
source: Strikingly, and in contrast to the previously reported homogenous distribution of E-cadherin along DV interfaces at mid-GBE (Blankenship et al., 2006), we found that E-cadherin was highly enriched at vertices (Figure 1A, B and C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: E-cadherin maintains a higher vertex:interface ratio than a control plasma membrane-associated marker (Gap43:mCh).
source: Systematic quantification of vertex-associated E-cadherin averaged across the entire time of GBE (see Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) also revealed that E-cadherin maintains a higher vertex:interface ratio than does a control, plasma membrane-associated marker (Gap43:mCh; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Vertex associated E-cadherin undergoes cycles of enrichment and dispersion.
source: Interestingly, although E-cadherin is enriched at vertices, it possesses a much wider distribution of intensities than the control marker, which suggested that vertex associated E-cadherin might undergo cycles of enrichment and dispersion (Figure 1C). Analysis of vertex E-cadherin confirmed that the intensity of enrichment fluctuates in time (Figure 1E and F; Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging and quantification in Figure 1E, F and Video 1.

claim: The vertex-specific localization of E-cadherin temporally coincides with intercalary movements.
source: These results show that the vertex-specific localization of E-cadherin temporally coincides with intercalary movements, and suggest that vertex E-cadherin may function in directing GBE.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal correlation observed in the data.

claim: The inward movement of vertices connected by a contracting interface does not show evidence of mechanical coupling.
source: A central physical expectation from previously described line-tension models (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Rauzi et al., 2010) is that the inward movement of vertices connected by a contracting interface should show evidence of mechanical coupling (Figure 2A). Surprisingly, however, we observed no evidence of this hypothesized coupling (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from systematic pair-wise analyses shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Physical coupling of vertices could only be observed in radial directions.
source: Indeed, in systematic pair-wise analyses of cell vertices, physical coupling could only be observed in radial directions (e.g. between vertices 3 and 6; Figure 2B' and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cross-correlation analysis in Figure 2B' and C.

claim: An inward correlation of vertex motion was only found between vertex pairs on opposite sides of the cell, with the largest correlations between those diametrically opposed.
source: In other words, an inward correlation of vertex motion was only found between vertex pairs on opposite sides of the cell, with the largest correlations between those diametrically opposed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown through quantitative analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: During the contraction of an AP interface, the motion of the two vertices toward the middle of the interface occurs independently of each other.
source: These results indicate that during the contraction of an AP interface, the motion of the two vertices toward the middle of the interface (referred to as 'productive' motion) occurs independently of each other, while all vertices undergo coupled motion into the radial direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: All vertices undergo coupled motion into the radial direction.
source: These results indicate that during the contraction of an AP interface, the motion of the two vertices toward the middle of the interface (referred to as 'productive' motion) occurs independently of each other, while all vertices undergo coupled motion into the radial direction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the radial correlation analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Cell vertices associated with contracting interfaces often underwent periods of productive sliding along the plasma membrane.
source: As we continued our analysis of vertex steps in vivo, a novel behavior began to emerge: cell vertices associated with contracting interfaces often underwent periods of productive sliding along the plasma membrane (Figure 2D; Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: As a vertical interface contracts, the interface adjacent to it elongates, and consequently the total length stays constant.
source: Measurement of interface lengths showed that as a vertical interface contracts (Figure 2D and E; blue) the interface adjacent to it elongates (Figure 2D and E; red), and consequently the total length stays constant (Figure 2D and E; black).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The compensatory increase in adjacent interface length is contrary to what would be expected through canonical models of interface contraction.
source: This compensatory increase in adjacent interface length is contrary to what would be expected through canonical models of interface contraction, in which the contracting interface shortens while adjacent interfaces maintain a constant length.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the observed behavior to expectations from existing models.

claim: The compensatory length behavior is a systematic component of T1-associated vertex movements.
source: Additionally, analysis of the lengths of all contracting and adjacent interfaces throughout GBE demonstrated that this behavior is a systematic component of T1-associated vertex movements (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown through systematic analysis of all contracting interfaces in Figure 2F.

claim: Vertices can take turns sliding over the course of a T1 contraction.
source: We also observe instances where vertices take turns sliding over the course of a T1 contraction (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-series analysis in Figure 2G and H.

claim: A single vertex can independently produce the changes in cell shape that drive cell intercalation.
source: These results are consistent with the observed, uncoupled movement of vertices, and provide a mechanism by which a single vertex can independently produce the changes in cell shape that drive cell intercalation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference drawn from the vertex sliding observations.

claim: An apical actomyosin network drives area oscillations during GBE.
source: Previous research has shown that an apical actomyosin network drives area oscillations during GBE (Rauzi et al., 2010; Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011); Figure 3A and A'; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by observations in Figure 3A, A' and Video 3.

claim: Apical area oscillations occur in the invagination of the Drosophila ventral furrow.
source: This appears to be a common feature of many cell shaping processes, as similar apical area oscillations occur in the invagination of the Drosophila ventral furrow (Martin et al., 2009; Roh-Johnson et al., 2012), neuroblast ingression (Simões et al., 2017; An et al., 2017), and the internalization of the C. elegans endodermal precursor cells (Roh-Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: About 64% of the effective length contraction of vertical interfaces occurs during area contraction, while only 36% occurs during area expansion.
source: These results show that about 64% of the effective length contraction of vertical interfaces occurs during area contraction, while only 36% occurs during area expansion when absolute length is stabilized (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the fractional length analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Vertex sliding occurs opportunistically during area contraction phases in a ratchet-like fashion, so that shortened vertical interface lengths are stabilized during area expansion.
source: Thus, vertex sliding occurs opportunistically during area contraction phases in a ratchet-like fashion, so that shortened vertical interface lengths are stabilized during area expansion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the phase-based length analysis.

claim: Cells possess concave cell contours during contraction, and convex boundaries during apical area expansion.
source: Interestingly, cells possess concave cell contours during contraction, and convex boundaries during apical area expansion (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the cell shape metric analysis in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Cell vertices, but not cell interfaces, lead overall changes in cell shape.
source: These results are consistent with cell vertices, but not cell interfaces, leading overall changes in cell shape and again suggest that cell vertices are key structures that govern cell topologies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell contour analysis.

claim: As cell areas contracted, vertex-associated E-cadherin intensity systematically increased.
source: A cross-correlation function relating E-cadherin intensity and cell area showed that as areas decreased, vertex-associated E-cadherin intensity systematically increased (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–A''').
evidence: This is demonstrated through cross-correlation analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Vertex E-cadherin intensity peaks just before cell area is in its most contracted state and before the onset of area expansion.
source: Interestingly, this cross-correlation also showed that vertex E-cadherin intensity peaks just before cell area is in its most contracted state and before the onset of area expansion (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown through the cross-correlation analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: E-cadherin intensity is coordinated with cell area oscillations.
source: Together, this phase relationship suggests that E-cadherin intensity is coordinated with cell area oscillations, and that enrichment of E-cadherin acts to stabilize sliding vertices.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal correlation between E-cadherin intensity and cell area.

claim: Enrichment of E-cadherin acts to stabilize sliding vertices.
source: Together, this phase relationship suggests that E-cadherin intensity is coordinated with cell area oscillations, and that enrichment of E-cadherin acts to stabilize sliding vertices.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference from the correlation between E-cadherin enrichment and interface length stabilization.

claim: Area oscillations provide the force for intercalation, with E-cadherin dynamics functioning as a molecular ratchet to harness vertex-sliding into productive movement.
source: These results further indicate a model in which area oscillations provide the force for intercalation, with E-cadherin dynamics functioning as a molecular ratchet to harness vertex-sliding into productive movement.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of multiple experimental findings.

claim: Inhibiting endocytosis by injecting embryos with chlorpromazine increased the total amount of E-cadherin at cell vertices and interfaces compared to control embryos.
source: We therefore inhibited endocytosis by injecting embryos with a small-molecule inhibitor, chlorpromazine (Levayer et al., 2011). This increased the total amount of E-cadherin at cell vertices and interfaces compared to control embryos; additionally, cells maintained a vertex-associated enrichment of E-cadherin throughout GBE (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the chlorpromazine injection experiment shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Endocytic inhibition prevented E-cadherin from oscillating to a lower enrichment state.
source: Importantly, endocytic inhibition prevented E-cadherin from oscillating to a lower enrichment state (Figure 4E and F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of E-cadherin dynamics in chlorpromazine-treated embryos in Figure 4E, F and Video 4.

claim: Oscillations in cell areas still occurred under endocytic inhibition conditions.
source: Although E-cadherin dynamics were disrupted, oscillations in cell areas still occurred (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B; Video 4).
evidence: This is shown through area oscillation measurements in chlorpromazine-treated embryos in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Under endocytic inhibition conditions, there was virtually no difference between the theoretical isotropic length change and the observed length changes for either vertical or transverse interfaces.
source: However, under these conditions we found that there was virtually no difference between the theoretical isotropic length change and the observed length changes for either vertical or transverse interfaces (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through interface length analysis in chlorpromazine-treated embryos in Figure 4G.

claim: Vertices in Ubiquitin-E-cadherin:GFP overexpressing embryos had displacements that were reduced by 41% as compared to control embryos.
source: Indeed, vertices in Ubiquitin-E-cadherin:GFP overexpressing embryos had displacements that were reduced by 41% as compared to control embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C'').
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the E-cadherin overexpression experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C''.

claim: Stabilizing E-cadherin prevents vertex sliding and uncouples the ratcheted motion of individual vertices from the motive oscillations in cell area.
source: Thus, stabilizing E-cadherin prevents vertex sliding and uncouples the ratcheted motion of individual vertices from the motive oscillations in cell area.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chlorpromazine and E-cadherin overexpression experiments.

claim: Increased E-cadherin levels restrict vertex sliding.
source: This further suggests that increased E-cadherin levels restrict vertex sliding, and supports a model in which E-cadherin enrichment at the end of an apical area oscillation serves as a ratchet that stabilizes vertices post-sliding.
evidence: This is an inference from the E-cadherin stabilization experiments.

claim: E-cadherin enrichment at the end of an apical area oscillation serves as a ratchet that stabilizes vertices post-sliding.
source: This further suggests that increased E-cadherin levels restrict vertex sliding, and supports a model in which E-cadherin enrichment at the end of an apical area oscillation serves as a ratchet that stabilizes vertices post-sliding.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by the experimental data.

claim: Productive displacements occurred when both cells A and B (the two AP neighboring cells at a T1 interface) were contracting.
source: When tangential displacement rates were plotted with the phases of cells A and B (the two AP neighboring cells at a T1 interface, Figure 5C'), productive displacements occurred when both cells were contracting (Figure 5C, C', E and E').
evidence: This is demonstrated through phase-based displacement analysis in Figure 5C, C', E and E'.

claim: Productive displacements only occurred during the coordinated expansion of cell C with the contraction of cell A.
source: However, when the phases of cells A and C were examined, productive displacements only occurred during the coordinated expansion of cell C with the contraction of cell A (Figure 5D, D', E and E').
evidence: This is shown through phase-based displacement analysis in Figure 5D, D', E and E'.

claim: The magnitude of displacement was much greater when cell C expanded while cell A contracted than when both cells A and B contracted.
source: Strikingly, the magnitude of displacement was much greater in this latter condition than in the first condition (Figure 5E and E').
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 5E and E'.

claim: The phase of cell C is more predictive of productive vertex sliding events than cells A or B.
source: This demonstrates that the phase of cell C is more predictive of productive vertex sliding events than cells A or B, and provides a mechanism for how anisotropic, radial force balance between three cells sharing a common vertex could couple individual T1-associated vertex steps to cell area oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phase-based displacement analysis.

claim: Anisotropic, radial force balance between three cells sharing a common vertex could couple individual T1-associated vertex steps to cell area oscillations.
source: This demonstrates that the phase of cell C is more predictive of productive vertex sliding events than cells A or B, and provides a mechanism for how anisotropic, radial force balance between three cells sharing a common vertex could couple individual T1-associated vertex steps to cell area oscillations.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference from the three-cell phase analysis.

claim: E-cadherin is specifically recruited to contracting vertices during apical cell area oscillations.
source: These results demonstrate that E-cadherin is specifically recruited to contracting vertices during apical cell area oscillations and suggest a mechanism to achieve anisotropic stabilization of vertex movements.
evidence: This is shown through the angle-resolved phase analysis in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Only contractile, T1-associated vertices show the maximal intensity increases that peak at the end of area contractions, while DV-associated vertices experienced reduced E-cadherin recruitment.
source: Indeed, only contractile, T1-associated vertices show the maximal intensity increases that peak at the end of area contractions, while DV-associated vertices experienced reduced E-cadherin recruitment (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through angle-resolved intensity analysis in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Stabilizing E-cadherin by disrupting endocytosis reduced the correlation between area phase and vertex movements.
source: Stabilizing E-cadherin by disrupting endocytosis reduced the correlation between area phase and vertex movements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), again consistent with E-cadherin dynamics directing productive vertex sliding events.
evidence: This is shown through phase-based displacement analysis in chlorpromazine-treated embryos in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myosin II is highly, and dynamically, enriched at vertices.
source: Simultaneous imaging of Myosin II:mCherry and E-cad:GFP revealed that, in addition to its previously described junctional and medial populations, Myosin II is highly, and dynamically, enriched at vertices (Figure 6A–A''; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B–B'' with Zipper:GFP).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 6A-A'' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vertex-associated Myosin II exhibited a strong colocalization with vertex-associated E-cadherin.
source: This unexpected population of Myosin II exhibited a strong colocalization with vertex-associated E-cadherin (Figure 6A and A').
evidence: This is shown through dual-channel imaging in Figure 6A and A'.

claim: The dynamics of enrichment of vertex Myosin II and vertex E-cadherin are temporally coupled.
source: Furthermore, systematic quantitation of vertex Myosin II and vertex E-cadherin demonstrated a strong cross-correlation, showing that the dynamics of enrichment of both proteins are temporally coupled (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–C''', D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cross-correlation analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Myosin II becomes enriched at vertices about 3.3 s before E-cadherin.
source: Interestingly, this cross-correlation function also revealed a slight temporal offset, with Myosin II becoming enriched at vertices about 3.3 s before E-cadherin (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-correlation analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Myosin II enrichment during periods of cell area contraction is polarized to T1 associated vertices.
source: Similar to E-cadherin (Figure 5G), phase-based analysis of Myosin II indicated an enrichment during periods of cell area contraction that is polarized to T1 associated vertices (Figure 6C and C'; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E with Zipper:GFP).
evidence: This is shown through angle-resolved phase analysis in Figure 6C and C'.

claim: Myosin II dynamics at vertices temporally precede those of E-cadherin.
source: However, these dynamics again subtly preceded those of E-cadherin (compare Figure 6C and C' and Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is shown through comparison of phase-based analyses in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Approximately 50% of medial Myosin II flows moved toward vertices, resulting in vertex enrichment.
source: As was previously described for interfaces (Rauzi et al., 2010), live imaging of individual cell behaviors showed that approximately 50% of medial Myosin II flows moved toward vertices, resulting in vertex enrichment (Figure 6D and E, and Video 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from live imaging analysis shown in Figure 6D, E and Video 5.

claim: Myosin II dynamics at vertices are similar to, but temporally precede, those of E-cadherin.
source: Taken together, these observations show that Myosin II dynamics at vertices are similar to, but temporally precede, those of E-cadherin, and suggest a role for Myosin II in clustering E-cadherin at vertices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal correlation and phase analyses.

claim: Myosin II plays a role in clustering E-cadherin at vertices.
source: Taken together, these observations show that Myosin II dynamics at vertices are similar to, but temporally precede, those of E-cadherin, and suggest a role for Myosin II in clustering E-cadherin at vertices.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal relationship between Myosin II and E-cadherin dynamics.

claim: Injection of a high concentration of Y-27632 (100 mM) disrupted E-cadherin enrichment to cell vertices, as well as E-cadherin dynamics.
source: To investigate if Myosin II is required for vertex-associated E-cadherin behaviors, we functionally disrupted Myosin II by injection of the Rok inhibitor Y-27632. Injection of a high concentration of Y-27632 (100 mM) disrupted E-cadherin enrichment to cell vertices, as well as E-cadherin dynamics (Figures 7A, C and E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Y-27632 injection experiment shown in Figures 7A, C and E.

claim: Analysis of sqhAX mutant embryos produced a similar defect in vertex-associated E-cadherin.
source: Additionally, analysis of sqhAX mutant embryos produced a similar defect in vertex-associated E-cadherin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown through analysis of sqhAX mutant embryos in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The phenotype of Y-27632 injected embryos was dose dependent.
source: The phenotype of Y-27632 injected embryos was dose dependent, as injection of a lower concentration (25 mM Y-27632) preserved an enrichment of E-cadherin at cell vertices (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of different Y-27632 concentrations in Figure 7B and D.

claim: At 25 mM Y-27632, E-cadherin was not significantly polarized to T1 associated vertices, and it lacked cycles of vertex enrichment.
source: In this background, however, E-cadherin was not significantly polarized to T1 associated vertices, and it lacked cycles of vertex enrichment (Figures 7D, F and G).
evidence: This is shown through quantitative analysis in Figures 7D, F and G.

claim: Vertex displacement was severely disrupted in Y-27632 injected embryos at both concentrations.
source: As a consequence, vertex displacement was severely disrupted in Y-27632 injected embryos at both concentrations (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phase-based displacement analysis in Figure 7H and I.

claim: Although productive vertex displacements are observed in Y-27632 injected embryos, these displacements are offset by backwards displacements.
source: Interestingly, although productive vertex displacements are observed (Figure 7H and I, red areas), these displacements are offset by backwards displacements (Figure 7H and I, blue areas).
evidence: This is shown through the heat maps in Figure 7H and I.

claim: Cell area oscillations are highly disrupted in Y-27632 injected embryos.
source: It is additionally important to note that cell area oscillations are highly disrupted in Y-27632 injected embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), and that the observed lack of E-cadherin dynamics could represent a disruption of coupling between vertex populations of E-cadherin and medial actomyosin-dependent area oscillations.
evidence: This is shown through area oscillation analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Myosin II functions upstream of the ratchet-like behavior of E-cadherin at vertices.
source: These results are consistent with Myosin II functioning upstream of the ratchet-like behavior of E-cadherin at vertices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Y-27632 and sqhAX mutant experiments.

claim: Myosin II has a functional role in clustering E-cadherin at vertices and directing the stabilization of productive sliding movements.
source: Either way, these results are consistent with a functional role for Myosin II in clustering E-cadherin at vertices and directing the stabilization of productive sliding movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Myosin II perturbation experiments.

claim: Radial force coupling drives ratchet-like contractions of AP interfaces.
source: In summary, we have shown that radial force coupling drives ratchet-like contractions of AP interfaces.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Tricellular vertices represent a new functional unit capable of regulating cell topologies.
source: These results also introduce a new functional unit capable of regulating cell topologies – tricellular vertices.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Tricellular vertices slide laterally in response to medial force generation.
source: We identify a new mechanism driving cell shape remodeling, in which tricellular vertices slide laterally in response to medial force generation (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed mechanism illustrated in Figure 7J.

claim: Higher line tensions at AP interfaces direct distinct aspects of intercalary cell behaviors such as interface alignment along the DV axis, recoil velocities upon laser ablation, and boundary element behaviors.
source: While higher line tensions at AP interfaces clearly exist and direct distinct aspects of intercalary cell behaviors (such as interface alignment along the DV axis, recoil velocities upon laser ablation, and boundary element behaviors), it will be interesting to further explore the mechanisms regulating tricellular vertex function (Rauzi et al., 2008; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Tetley et al., 2016).
evidence: This acknowledges the role of line tensions while proposing additional mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Vertex displacement relies on the summed total of local force contributions from three (or more) interfaces as well as radial coupling.
source: As vertices are connected to three (or more) interfaces as well as the radial coupling reported on here, their displacement will rely on the summed total of these local force contributions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about how vertices integrate multiple force inputs.

claim: Endocytic uptake of plasma membrane and adhesion proteins at interfaces may contribute to biases in lateral vertex displacements.
source: Some of the mechanisms may involve the endocytic uptake of plasma membrane and adhesion proteins at interfaces which have been recently described (Levayer et al., 2011; Jewett et al., 2017). These molecular models of regulated adhesion are not necessarily dependent on line tensions, and could contribute to the biases in lateral vertex displacements in particular tangential directions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Local regions of either medial- or interface-associated Myosin II are likely to impact vertex displacements.
source: Although our data argue against a predominant function of interface-spanning line tensions in directing interface contraction, local regions of either medial- or interface-associated Myosin II are likely to impact vertex displacements as well.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential contributions of Myosin II to vertex displacement.

claim: By mid-GBE, interface localization of both E-cadherin and Myosin II significantly strengthen.
source: Indeed, although E-cadherin and Myosin II are primarily located at cell vertices early in GBE, by mid-GBE interface localization of both significantly strengthen and is consistent with interface as well as radial contributions to vertex displacements.
evidence: This is an observation about the temporal dynamics of protein localization.

claim: Cell vertices are well positioned to integrate the many different force-generating networks that will ultimately determine changes in cell shape and topology.
source: Thus, cell vertices are well positioned to integrate the many different force-generating networks that will ultimately determine changes in cell shape and topology.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion about the role of vertices.

claim: Intercellular adhesion dynamics are required for vertex movement.
source: Our results also show that intercellular adhesion dynamics are required for vertex movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the E-cadherin stabilization experiments.

claim: Under conditions in which E-cadherin exhibited greater enrichment and/or stability than in wild-type embryos, AP and transverse interface lengths oscillated identically.
source: Under conditions in which E-cadherin exhibited greater enrichment and/or stability than is present in wild-type embryos, AP and transverse interface lengths oscillated identically, suggesting that cell vertices were unable to slide productively due to increased adhesive stability.
evidence: This is an observation from the chlorpromazine and E-cadherin overexpression experiments.

claim: Cell vertices were unable to slide productively due to increased adhesive stability when E-cadherin was stabilized.
source: Under conditions in which E-cadherin exhibited greater enrichment and/or stability than is present in wild-type embryos, AP and transverse interface lengths oscillated identically, suggesting that cell vertices were unable to slide productively due to increased adhesive stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the interface length analysis in E-cadherin stabilization experiments.

claim: Endocytic events may underlie the dispersion phase of E-cadherin dynamics at cell vertices.
source: Stabilizing E-cadherin was achieved by inhibiting endocytosis (Levayer et al., 2011), and suggests that endocytic events may underlie the dispersion phase of E-cadherin dynamics at cell vertices.
evidence: This is an inference from the chlorpromazine experiment, supported by citation.

claim: As cells contract their apical area, E-cadherin and Myosin II are preferentially recruited to AP vertices to provide the adhesive force necessary to stabilize vertex position and interface length during area relaxation.
source: We have also shown that as cells contract their apical area, E-cadherin and Myosin II are preferentially recruited to AP vertices to provide the adhesive force necessary to stabilize vertex position and interface length during area relaxation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the phase-based analysis.

claim: Anisotropy in cell area oscillations and local imbalances in interface-associated forces are likely responsible for enforcing the directionality of intercalation.
source: This, as well as anisotropy in cell area oscillations and local imbalances in interface-associated forces (Rauzi et al., 2010; Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2011), are likely responsible for enforcing the directionality of intercalation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms of directionality, supported by citations.

claim: Vertex displacement has the strongest correlation with expansive motion in the adjacent, DV-oriented cells.
source: Our results also suggest that, while radial forces in cells sharing a contracting AP interface are important for vertex displacement, vertex displacement has the strongest correlation with expansive motion in the adjacent, DV-oriented cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the three-cell phase analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Adjacent cells provide motive force for interface extension rather than the cells that share the newly growing interface.
source: This is intriguing, and suggests a homology to recent results during interface extension in which the adjacent cells provide motive force for extension rather than the cells that share the newly growing interface (Collinet et al., 2015; Yu and Fernandez-Gonzalez, 2016).
evidence: This draws a parallel to previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: AP vs DV anisotropy at the level of vertices could be a result of stress anisotropy and a mechanosensory feedback loop.
source: At the molecular level, AP vs DV anisotropy at the level of vertices could be a result of stress anisotropy and a mechanosensory feedback loop.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Vertices may experience differentially positioned signaling networks, allowing for Myosin II and E-cadherin vertex enrichment.
source: Alternatively, vertices may also experience differentially positioned signaling networks, allowing for Myosin II and E-cadherin vertex enrichment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: A similar adherens junction sliding behavior has been observed during three dimensional epithelial folding events as well as during cell ordering in the Drosophila notum.
source: While the planar sliding behaviors described here are a novel mechanism underlying intercalary behaviors, it is also interesting to note that a similar adherens junction sliding behavior has been observed during three dimensional epithelial folding events as well as during cell ordering in the Drosophila notum (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Curran et al., 2017).
evidence: This draws parallels to other systems, supported by citations.

claim: In the formation of epithelial folds on the dorsal surface of the embryo, there is a basal shift in adherens junction position in response to Rap1 signaling events.
source: In the formation of the epithelial folds that occur on the dorsal surface of the embryo in response to GBE, there is a basal shift in adherens junction position in response to Rap1 signaling events (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the Drosophila pupal notum, a conservation of total junctional lengths, referred to as 'continuous neighbor exchange' has been observed.
source: It is also highly interesting that, in the Drosophila pupal notum, a similar conservation of total junctional lengths, referred to as 'continuous neighbor exchange' has been observed (Curran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The repositioning of junctional/vertex elements may represent a new and conserved paradigm in how cell topologies are re-shaped during development.
source: It may well be that the repositioning of junctional/vertex elements will represent a new and conserved paradigm in how cell topologies are re-shaped during development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: Cell vertices possess important molecular characteristics capable of coordinating complex cell morphologies.
source: Previous studies have shown that cell vertices possess important molecular characteristics capable of coordinating complex cell morphologies (Staehelin, 1973; Graf et al., 1982; Schulte et al., 2003; Ikenouchi et al., 2005; Blankenship et al., 2006; Byri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tricellular junctions act as key sensors of cell shape that serve as landmarks to orient epithelial cell divisions.
source: Indeed, recent work has shown that tricellular junctions act as key sensors of cell shape that serve as landmarks to orient epithelial cell divisions (Bosveld et al., 2016), and intestinal stem cells require tricellular function to maintain appropriate homeostatic levels (Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Intestinal stem cells require tricellular function to maintain appropriate homeostatic levels.
source: Indeed, recent work has shown that tricellular junctions act as key sensors of cell shape that serve as landmarks to orient epithelial cell divisions (Bosveld et al., 2016), and intestinal stem cells require tricellular function to maintain appropriate homeostatic levels (Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Vertices represent unique domains of the cell surface.
source: This suggests that vertices represent unique domains of the cell surface and that tricellular vertices have a special role as centers of functional signaling and physical networks within epithelial sheets.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion drawn from the study's findings and previous work.

claim: Tricellular vertices have a special role as centers of functional signaling and physical networks within epithelial sheets.
source: This suggests that vertices represent unique domains of the cell surface and that tricellular vertices have a special role as centers of functional signaling and physical networks within epithelial sheets.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion drawn from the study's findings and previous work.
